newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FEATURE - Hong Kong property sales to stay well bid.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Hong Kong property sales to stay well bid.

text.p: Hong Kong's property developers, undeterred by the imminent return of the British colony to Chinese rule, are set to shower the residential market with new apartments before the year is out.
And property analysts say demand is keen and buyers are seen bidding up prices well into 1997.
"Supply and demand look pretty good for the market and sentiment is going to be increasingly positive over the next 12 months," said Martin Tacon, senior associate at CS First Boston.
"We could be seeing in the region of a thousand units coming up between now and the end of the year," he said, adding that the sales should be accompanied by a small rise in prices.

Sun Hung Kai Properties Ltd said the public could register for a first batch of 36 units at its Kings Park Villa luxury residential development in Kowloon from December 2-4. It will have 360 units on offer at the development on completion.
The company also hopes to offer units at its East Point City development in Tseung Kwan O in the New Territories, where it will have 2,184 units.

Cheung Kong (Holdings) Ltd said it also hoped to get government approval to launch sales at its Laguna Verde development in Hung Hom in Kowloon. Phase one of the development will have five blocks of about 750 units on offer.

New World Development Co Ltd has a second batch of 1,120 units at Discovery Park in Tsuen Wan in the New Territories which it hopes to launch and analysts said Henderson Land Development Co Ltd still had units at its Metro City Development in Tseung Kwan O.

"We are actually looking at a lot of supply coming on stream from the big four developers. I think the big boys will still dominate the property scene over the next couple of months," said Carol Lai, research manager at SOCGEN-Crosby Securities.
SUPPLY CANNOT KEEP UP WITH DEMAND

But residential property supply has been unable to keep up with demand and analysts expect an upturn in property prices to continue for the remainder of 1996 and 1997, after a fall of some 10 to 30 percent in 1995 from the peaks of mid-1994.

"There is no supply," said Peter Churchouse, regional strategist at Morgan Stanley. "This year, private housing supply is going to be about 19,000 units. It will be about 26,000 to 27,000 next year versus a long term average of 30 to 32,000."
Churchouse said prices were set to rise about 20 percent over the next 12 months compared to a rise of between 15 and 20 percent between October 1995 and October 1996.

"What I am expecting to see is a small price rise in the mass residential market for the end of this year and I think we could see something in the region of a 20 percent rise in the next 12 months," added Tacon.

However, some industry experts have more moderate predictions. "A repetition of a sharp 20 or 30 percent (price) rise, which happened in the past, is unlikely because current (property) prices are already at a reasonable level," Henderson Land chairman Lee Shau-kee said recently.
"We expect (property) prices to edge up at a steady pace even after 1997, a pace more or less in line with inflation and depending on the condition of supply and demand in the market."

A recent report by Merrill Lynch estimated that residential property prices would grow at eight to 12 percent in each of the next two years. "As prices of new flats have already risen 25-35 percent since last September, we could probably see a long period of slow price increases of around 1-2 percent every 2-3 months through mid-1997," it said.
"Thereafter, continued short supply and strong user demand should underpin a positive long-term picture," Merrill added.

Lai also saw a slowdown in price rises in the residential market, with mass residential prices growing by some five to eight percent next year. But she said luxury residential properties were testing new highs and pointed to prices fetched by Sun Hung Kai Properties at its Harbourview development in Mid-Levels on Hong Kong island.
"There was a transaction at an unprecedented high of HK$17,500 (US$2,264) per square foot," she said. Lai expected luxury residential prices to rise 10-15 percent in 1997.

Hong Kong's property market is one of the most expensive in the world. "The only time you could ever say that Hong Kong was relatively cheap on a global scale, was about 1985 when prices had collapsed by 60 odd percent," said Churchouse.
"Even then it was on a per square foot basis still more expensive than London and New York and any of the other major cities in the world except Tokyo," he added.
Analysts said a number of factors pointed to a sustained recovery in the local property market.

"Household incomes are rising at 10 or 11 percent, interest rates are relatively modest and are not set to go up, banks are competing actively for mortage business... and you have got something over the next 18 months like 150,000 people expected to come into Hong Kong to live," said Churchouse.
INFLOW FROM MAINLAND EXPECTED AFTER HANDOVER
Hong Kong's return to Chinese rule in mid-1997 is expected to lead to an inflow of people from the mainland.
Churchouse also said that government consents to commence residential buildings were almost at record low levels.
A report by Salomon Brothers property analyst Michael Green said there had been a sharp rise in property speculation in the residential market in October and an upsurge in mainland Chinese buying.
"There has been no notable publicity of large deals, which suggests confidentiality. This, we believe, points towards a large increase in mainland Chinese buying," he said.
"The fact that 30 percent of applicants for a recent property development were company registrations, suggests a rise in speculative buying in the residential market for the month."

Bullish signs have also emerged recently in the sluggish office property market, with property investment company Hysan Development Ltd's purchase of a major property in Hong Kong's Central district at a price well above recent market rates.

Chinese Estates Holdings Ltd agreed to sell the entire 34-storey, 211,000 square foot Entertainment Building to Hysan for HK$3.64 billion. The building has six floors of retail space and 28 floors of office space.
Hysan said the value of the retail space was between HK$20,000 and HK$24,000 per square foot and the office space was about HK$15,000 per square foot.

"This transaction has confirmed people's views that the (property) investors are prepared to pay that sort of money for offices and rents are simply going to have to increase," said Tacon. "There does seem to be a short to medium term fundamentally strong argument for central, prime property."
